title: Tree-ring dating
hook: Tree rings can date a wooden beam to the exact year its tree was cut down.
peek: Wide and narrow rings record good and bad growing years, and trees across a region share the same pattern. Match that pattern, and a piece of old timber can be dated to the very year it grew.
lede: A tree adds one ring of wood each growing season, wide in a good year and narrow in a dry or cold one. Trees in the same region share the same run of good and bad years, so their rings form a matching barcode. Line up overlapping samples, from living trees back through old beams, and wood can be dated to the exact year.

bullets.text: An astronomer in Arizona, Douglass began studying rings in the early 1900s, hoping they held a record of sunspot cycles. Instead he built a new science, and in 1937 founded the University of Arizona's Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research.

For years Douglass had a gap between his living-tree record and the ruins of the American Southwest. In 1929 a charred beam found at Show Low, Arizona, bridged it and gave calendar dates to sites such as Pueblo Bonito.

Radiocarbon dating assumes a steady level of carbon-14 in the air, which is not quite true. Tree rings of known age supply the correction, and European oak and pine records now reach back more than 12,000 years.

Specialists date violin tops by matching their rings to records of Alpine spruce. The method has been used to check famous instruments credited to Stradivari, including the long-debated Messiah violin.
Tree-ring records across the Northern Hemisphere mark 1816 as one of the coldest summers in centuries, the year after Mount Tambora erupted.
